# EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents

###### Abstract

Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and
transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual
learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied
settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this
gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied
simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of
self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core
evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first
learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve
complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct
extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning
methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our
results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under
zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent
improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the
task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale
accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents
cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience.
Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental
yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable
resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied
environments. Our code and dataset are available at
[https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage](https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage).

## 1 Introduction

Self-evolving agents ([Gao et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Fang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)) can accumulate experience from past interactions and
progressively enhance their task performance without additional human
supervision. Such agents are capable of retaining and transferring
skills across tasks over time, a capability broadly termed *continual
learning* ([Zheng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib4)). This capability is
particularly important for embodied intelligence ([Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14); [Yifan et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib16)), where agents are expected to operate in complex,
ever-changing physical environments that cannot be fully anticipated at
training time. It is therefore important to develop a principled
approach for evaluating the capability to learn from prior interactions
and transfers the acquired skills to new tasks.

Existing benchmarks in continual learning and embodied intelligence
partially address this evaluation goal. Research on continual learning
has largely focused on non-embodied settings, including
knowledge-intensive tasks ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), interactive
digital environments ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)), and long-term
simulated worlds ([Cai et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). These platforms do
not capture the spatial complexity and physical constraints inherent in
embodied tasks. Meanwhile, embodied benchmarks evaluate capabilities
such as scene perception ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), visual
navigation ([Anderson et al., 2018](#bib.bib21)), robotic
manipulation ([Gu et al., 2023](#bib.bib28)), and long-horizon task
planning ([Shridhar et al., 2020](#bib.bib31)), but are not specifically
designed to assess continual learning. Therefore, there remains a lack
of a dedicated benchmark for evaluating whether self-evolving agents can
accumulate experience and transfer it to solve novel tasks in embodied
environments.

To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark
in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability
of self-evolving agents. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
our design stems from compositional generalization ([Furuta et al.,
2023](#bib.bib41); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)). Instead of learning
every new task from scratch, a self-evolving agent should recombine
previously acquired skill elements to solve novel, unseen tasks. We thus
consider compositional generalization as a principled way to measure
agent continual learning capability. Specifically, we first assign a set
of basic tasks for the agent to execute and learn the skills. We then
test whether the agent can effectively leverage such experience to solve
unseen advanced tasks that require recombining the learned skills. From
this perspective, basic tasks serve as test-time learning ([Sun et al.,
2020](#bib.bib55); [Liu et al., 2021](#bib.bib56)) data for the agent to
build experience before attempting advanced tasks. To this end,
EmbodiedCLBench organizes tasks into three compositional levels:
(1) atomic actions from TongSim ([Sun et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)),
representing basic object–action interactions; (2) basic tasks, with
each composing a small number of atomic actions into practical household
operations across multiple categories; and (3) advanced tasks, with each
combining elements from multiple basic-task categories.

![Refer to caption](2610.13021v1/tongbench_self_evolution_intro.png)

Figure 1: Compositional generalization is leveraged as a principled way
to measure continual learning capability. An agent that has experience
from basic tasks should recombine previously acquired skills to solve
novel, unseen advanced tasks, rather than learning each new task from
scratch.

Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive evaluation across
multiple agent harnesses (e.g., OpenClaw and Codex) and learning methods
(In-Context Learning and Skill Learning). Our results reveal several
notable and, in some cases, unexpected findings. First, while advanced
tasks can hardly be solved in the zero-shot setting, agents with
experience from related basic tasks achieve substantially higher success
rates. This validates that experience from simpler tasks can be
effectively transferred to unseen, harder tasks. Second, the performance
gain over zero-shot agents remains at a stable level as task complexity
increases. This suggests that continual learning capability is not
sensitive to task difficulty. Third, the improvement from learning does
not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples. A single
basic task significantly improves performance, and additional samples
yield no consistent further improvement. Fourth, past experience
facilitates the decision behavior of agents by selecting more meaningful
actions with fewer unexecutable ones.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied
  simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of
  self-evolving agents.
- •
  Our key innovation lies in leveraging compositional generalization as
  a principled way to construct tasks, design evaluation protocols, and
  evaluate continual learning capability.
- •
  We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across multiple agent harnesses
  and learning methods, revealing limitations of current agents and
  providing insights for future design.

## 2 Related Work

#### Continual Learning Benchmarks.

Evaluating continual learning capabilities has become an increasingly
active topic for LLMs and agents ([Gao et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Fang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Zheng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib4)). Existing
benchmarks span several distinct domains. In knowledge-intensive tasks,
prior work evaluates whether agents can effectively transfer procedural
experience across coding, reasoning, and question-answering tasks ([Gao
et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Shu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)). In interactive digital environments, benchmarks test
continual learning capabilities in web automation, operating systems,
and knowledge graphs ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Zheng et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib9)). In long-term simulated environments, benchmarks
model persistent virtual worlds where past behaviors continuously shape
future states and decisions ([Cai et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). Another
major direction focuses on skill-centric evolution, studying whether
agents can abstract reusable skills from experience and transfer them
across tasks ([Zhong et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Guan et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Lei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib57)). Despite this progress, these benchmarks primarily
operate in digital or symbolic environments, leaving continual learning
in embodied scenarios largely unexplored.

#### Embodied AI Benchmarks.

Embodied AI benchmarks evaluate the capabilities ranging from perception
to long-horizon task execution ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib14); [Yifan
et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib16)). At the
perception level, benchmarks test 3D scene understanding ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), spatial reasoning ([Du et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)),
physical world understanding ([Chow et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)), and
scene dynamics ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). For navigation, the
field has progressed from language-conditioned navigation ([Anderson et
al., 2018](#bib.bib21); [Ku et al., 2020](#bib.bib22)) to sound-guided
navigation [Liu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1), object grounding ([Qi et al.,
2020](#bib.bib23)), multi-modal lifelong navigation ([Khanna et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24)), and active exploration for question
answering ([Majumdar et al., 2024](#bib.bib25)). In manipulation,
benchmarks evaluate multi-task generalization ([Yu et al.,
2020](#bib.bib26); [James et al., 2020](#bib.bib27)), object-level skill
transfer ([Gu et al., 2023](#bib.bib28)), lifelong knowledge
transfer ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib29)), and everyday task
scalability ([Nasiriany et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)). For long-horizon
planning, benchmarks require agents to follow compositional
instructions ([Shridhar et al., 2020](#bib.bib31)), interact through
dialogue ([Padmakumar et al., 2021](#bib.bib32)), compose
language-conditioned skills ([Mees et al., 2022](#bib.bib33)), handle
diverse household activities ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib34)), and adapt
plans based on visual feedback ([Tupini et al., 2026](#bib.bib35)).
These benchmarks comprehensively cover perception, navigation,
manipulation, and planning. Recent works further explore general-purpose
embodied agent evaluation and realistic simulation environments ([Peng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib58); [Ren et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)). However,
none is designed for evaluating the continual learning capability of
skills in long-horizon tasks.

#### Compositional Generalization.

Compositional generalization, the ability to recombine learned elements
for solving novel problems, has been studied across multiple domains. In
digital environments, benchmarks test whether mobile and web agents can
compose atomic operations into multi-step tasks ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40); [Furuta et al., 2023](#bib.bib41)). In video
understanding, benchmarks study whether models can recognize unseen
action–object combinations from separately learned components ([Li et
al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Ahn et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)). For reasoning
tasks, benchmarks show that models proficient in individual abilities
still fail when these abilities must be combined ([Alazraki et al.,
2026](#bib.bib42); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib43)). In embodied
manipulation, benchmarks evaluate whether robot policies can generalize
to unseen skill compositions after training on atomic skills ([Wu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib37); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib38); [Haresh et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)). In contrast,
EmbodiedCLBench evaluates the continual learning capability in embodied
simulation without any benchmark-specific training.

## 3 Benchmark Construction

As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Environment Setup: Embodied Simulation ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
the construction of EmbodiedCLBench consists of four stages:
(1) environment setup, (2) task generation, (3) graph construction, and
(4) evaluation protocol. We introduce each stage in the following
subsections.

### 3.1 Environment Setup: Embodied Simulation

Evaluating compositional generalization requires a large combinatorial
space of object–action pairs. We thus adopt TongSim as the simulation
platform ([Sun et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)). It provides a controllable
environment that supports rich physical interactions and scales to
diverse task configurations. It was also used in recent embodied agent
evaluation studies ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib47); [Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48)).

Specifically, TongSim is a simulation with household scenarios and
supports a wide range of interactive objects (such as cups, plates,
cabinets, lamps, and appliances) and executable actions (such as walk
to, look at, pick up, put down, open, close, and switch on, etc.). This
simulation offers three key advantages: (1) the platform supports a
large number of object types and action primitives, providing sufficient
combinatorial diversity; (2) all scenes are indoor domestic
environments, so that the tasks are grounded in meaningful, real-world
household activities; and (3) TongSim has not been widely used as
training data for existing foundation models, making it suitable for
evaluating the generalization capability of agents with reduced risk of
data contamination.

![Refer to
caption](2610.13021v1/tongbench_pipeline_overview_lrx_refine.png)

Figure 2: Overview of the construction process of EmbodiedCLBench.
During task generation, basic tasks connect a few atomic actions into
simple household operations, and advanced tasks combine elements from
multiple basic tasks into compositional tasks. For each task, a
state-transition graph is built, with each graph node as an intermediate
state and paired with action options and a first-person-view image.
During evaluation, the agent observes the current state and selects from
candidate actions. After each selection, the agent transitions to the
next node on the graph.

### 3.2 Task Generation: Compositional Generalization

Our goal is to evaluate the capability of continual learning. However,
it is an abstract concept that is challenging to measure directly. We
operationalize it through compositional generalization: if an agent has
learned from basic tasks, it should recombine previously mastered skill
elements to solve novel tasks rather than learning each new task from
scratch. This leads to a natural evaluation protocol—let the agent first
complete simpler tasks to accumulate experience, then test whether it
can leverage that experience to solve more complex, unseen tasks.

We design two levels of tasks based on atomic actions available in
TongSim. Specifically, an atomic action is a single interaction with an
object (e.g., “pick up the cup”). It consists of a sequence of steps
(e.g., walking to the cup, looking at it, and picking it up), each of
which is one executable action. Building on it, a basic task composes a
small number of atomic actions into a practical household operation
(e.g., “put the cup on the table”, which consists of “pick up the cup”
and “put down the cup on the table”). Further, an advanced task composes
more atomic actions than a basic task (e.g., “tidy up the room”, which
requires picking up the book, putting the book on the shelf, closing the
cabinet, and switching off the lamp). We provide more details in the
benchmark overview
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")).
All task descriptions are generated by Qwen3.7-Plus and manually
verified for correctness (see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Graph Construction Pipeline ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")).

### 3.3 Graph Construction: Action Trajectory Annotation

For TongSim simulation, we chose its closed-source version, which
provides more diverse actions than the open-source version. As a result,
online simulation is not practical for the benchmark evaluation.
Therefore, we construct an offline, reproducible evaluation process in
the form of a state-transition graph, as shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Environment Setup: Embodied Simulation ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents").
A graph structure naturally represents the task procedure: at each
state, an agent selects an action and transitions to the next state.
This graph structure offers three advantages: (1) offline evaluation can
be run in parallel without running the simulator; (2) flexible control
over the task complexity through graph branching and depth; and
(3) fine-grained analysis of agent behavior by checking each decision
against the pre-computed graph.

Specifically, each graph node represents a unique environment state
(e.g., “near the desk and looking at the lamp”). It is paired with an
image captured from TongSim and a set of action candidates presented to
the agent during evaluation. These candidates are generated by
Qwen3.7-Plus and manually verified for correctness. Each executable
candidate corresponds to an edge that deterministically transitions to
the next state. Given a task, we first define its initial and goal
states and then use breadth-first search to find the shortest path
between them. Since each state supports only a bounded set of objects
and actions, the reachable state space is compact enough for reliable
graph search. We construct the distractor paths by expanding alternative
executable actions from nodes along the shortest path. These paths are
executable but deviate from the shortest path. The detailed construction
pipeline and task examples are provided in
Appendices [B](#A2 "Appendix B Graph Construction Pipeline ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
and [C](#A3 "Appendix C Task Examples ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents").

### 3.4 Evaluation Protocol

With the task graphs built, we define how agents are evaluated on them.
The evaluation consists of a learning phase and a testing phase. In the
learning phase, the agent completes basic tasks to accumulate
experience. In the testing phase, the agent attempts unseen advanced
tasks with this experience. In this setup, basic tasks serve as the
memory ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib60); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib61))
and test-time learning data ([Sun et al., 2020](#bib.bib55); [Liu et
al., 2021](#bib.bib56)) for the self-evolving agents.

For each task, the evaluation follows an interactive, multi-turn format:
(1) the agent receives a task description and an image of the initial
state; (2) at each step, the agent selects one action from a set of
action candidates; (3) based on the action decision, the agent
transitions to the next state and receives a new image with updated
objects and action candidates; (4) this repeats until the agent reaches
the goal (success) or exhausts the step budget (failure). The action
candidates at each step are designed into three types: optimal actions
that follow the shortest path, suboptimal actions that are executable
but deviate from the shortest path, and invalid actions that cannot be
executed in the current state. This interactive format preserves the
sequential decision-making structure of embodied tasks while enabling
fully offline, deterministic, and reproducible evaluation.

## 4 Main Experiments

In this section, we first describe the experimental setup, including the
benchmark overview, evaluation settings, agent configurations, and
metrics. We then report and discuss the main results.

![Refer to caption](2610.13021v1/tongbench_benchmark_statistics.png)

Figure 3: Benchmark statistics of EmbodiedCLBench: environment
configuration (a), task composition across six categories (b), and task
complexity at two levels (c).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmark overview.

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
summarizes the overall statistics of EmbodiedCLBench. The environment
covers diverse scenes, object categories, and atomic actions, providing
a broad combinatorial space for task construction. The benchmark
contains 268 tasks: 168 basic tasks and 100 advanced tasks. Basic tasks
span six categories, with each grounded in a distinct type of daily
household activity. Advanced tasks require substantially more atomic
actions and shortest-path steps. The atomic actions of each advanced
task come from two to four categories of basic tasks. Each atomic action
consists of 3 steps. Therefore, the shortest path has 6 steps for a
basic task (2 atomic actions) and 12 steps for an advanced task (4
atomic actions). With this scale, real-world grounding, and structured
difficulty, EmbodiedCLBench can reveal meaningful differences in the
continual learning capability of agents. Examples of basic and advanced
tasks are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Task Examples ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents").

#### Evaluation settings.

We evaluate agents under three settings: (1) Zero-shot: the agent
performs basic and advanced tasks directly, without a learning phase.
(2) In-Context Learning (ICL): in the learning phase, the agent
completes two related basic tasks for each advanced task. In the testing
phase, the full interaction trajectories of these basic tasks are
retained in context. (3) Skill Learning: in the learning phase, the
agent completes the same basic tasks as in ICL. It then writes a concise
skill summary of its experience in Markdown format. In the testing
phase, only this skill summary is provided in context, instead of the
interaction trajectories.

The step budget of each task is the length of its shortest path plus
extra steps. In the testing phase, we allow 3 extra steps as a small
tolerance for suboptimal decisions. In the learning phase, we allow 6
extra steps for more exploration.

#### Agent configurations.

We evaluate all tasks under each of four agent harnesses:
OpenClaw ([OpenClaw, 2026](#bib.bib49)), Claude Code ([Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib50)), Codex ([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib51)), and
Hermes ([Nous Research, 2026](#bib.bib52)). We pair each harness with
two backbone models through their official APIs: Qwen3.8-Flash ([Qwen,
2026](#bib.bib53)) and GPT5.6-Terra ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib54)).

#### Metrics.

We report Success Rate (SR), which measures whether an agent can
complete a task within the allotted step budget:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{SR}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}\,,\quad c_{i}\in\{0,1\}\text{ indicates whether task }i\text{ is completed.}
``` |  | (1) |

Success rate directly reflects continual learning capability—whether
accumulated experience enables the agent to solve novel, compositionally
harder tasks.

### 4.2 Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Agent configurations. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
presents the main results. Agents achieve a moderate zero-shot success
rate on basic tasks (around 50%), indicating that current agents can
execute simple household tasks. Zero-shot success rate on advanced tasks
drops to around 10%, validating that advanced tasks are genuinely
difficult. Both ICL and Skill Learning substantially improve advanced
task success rate, raising it from around 10% to above 30%. This
improvement is consistent across all harnesses, suggesting that
experience from basic tasks can effectively transfer to unseen advanced
tasks.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Discussion.

Between ICL and Skill Learning, there is no consistent advantage of one
over the other. We conjecture that both methods can extract meaningful
information from the agent experience. Besides, the performance across
harnesses is close yet far from saturation, suggesting great potential
for improvement. Designing harnesses for continual learning can be a
future direction.

## 5 Analysis

### 5.1 Effects of Compositional Complexity

#### Motivation and Setting.

Compositional generalization is the core approach for evaluating
continual learning in EmbodiedCLBench. A natural question follows: does
more complex composition make continual learning harder? In the main
experiment, advanced tasks consist of 4 atomic actions. Here, we extend
our evaluation data to advanced tasks with 3 to 6 atomic actions to
control compositional complexity. We measure both the raw success rate
at each level and the gain over zero shot, defined as the success rate
of In-Context Learning or Skill Learning minus the zero-shot success
rate. We use Hermes with Qwen3.8-Flash for this analysis.

![Refer to
caption](2610.13021v1/figure/experiment/L_N/L_N_complexity.png)

Figure 4: Effect of compositional complexity on continual learning. The
$`x`$-axis varies the number of atomic actions per advanced task from 3
to 6. (a) reports the raw success rate achieved by each setting.
(b) reports the gain over zero shot, defined as the success rate of ICL
or Skill Learning minus that of zero shot, isolating the improvement
attributed to the learning phase.

#### Results and Analysis.

As shown in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Motivation and Setting. ‣ 5.1 Effects of Compositional Complexity ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")(a),
success rate decreases across all three settings as atomic actions
increase from 3 to 6. The largest drop occurs between 3 and 4 atomic
actions (e.g., ICL falls from 72.0% to 42.0%), after which the success
rate levels off. In the zero-shot setting, success rate decreases
sharply (e.g., from 28.0% to 4.0%). In contrast, ICL and Skill Learning
remain more stable in relative terms. Specifically,
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Motivation and Setting. ‣ 5.1 Effects of Compositional Complexity ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")(b)
shows that the gain over zero shot drops initially but then stabilizes
at around 30%. This indicates that experience from basic tasks remains
helpful as compositional complexity increases. At the highest complexity
(6 atomic actions), zero-shot success rate drops to 4.0%, while ICL and
Skill Learning still achieve 32.0% and 26.0%, respectively. This shows
that experience from basic tasks still brings a substantial gain over
zero shot, even when zero-shot agents can barely solve the tasks.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.2 Scaling with the Number of Learning Samples

#### Motivation and Setting.

Continual learning assumes that accumulated experience improves an
agent’s performance on harder tasks. If this holds, more experience
should lead to a higher success rate on advanced tasks. In the main
experiment, agents learn from 2 basic tasks before attempting advanced
tasks. Here, we increase the number of learning samples (i.e., basic
tasks in the learning phase) from $`k{=}0`$ (zero shot) to $`k{=}6`$. We
measure the success rate on the same set of advanced tasks under both
In-Context Learning and Skill Learning settings. We evaluate two agent
harnesses, Hermes and OpenClaw, both using Qwen3.8-Flash as the backbone
model.

![Refer to
caption](2610.13021v1/figure/experiment/n_sample/n_sample_extra_steps_3.png)

Figure 5: Success rate versus the number of learning samples. Each
learning sample is a basic task that the agent completes before being
tested on advanced tasks.

Results and Analysis. As shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Motivation and Setting. ‣ 5.2 Scaling with the Number of Learning Samples ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
the most substantial improvement occurs between $`k{=}0`$ and $`k{=}1`$.
A single learning sample raises the success rate from 8.0%–10.0% to
28.0%–40.0% across both harnesses and learning methods. This initial
jump accounts for most of the total improvement across the $`k`$ range.
Even minimal experience (completing just one basic task) provides
sufficient new information for the agent to substantially improve on
unseen advanced tasks. Beyond $`k{=}1`$, however, success rate does not
continue to rise but instead fluctuates without a clear upward trend.
This pattern remains across ICL and Skill Learning, and across both
harnesses. None of the four curves shows consistent improvement with
additional learning samples. This suggests that current agents cannot
extract sufficiently distinct information from additional learning
samples. Therefore, scalable continual learning, where success rate
keeps improving as learning samples increase, remains an open challenge
for embodied agents.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to
caption](2610.13021v1/figure/experiment/action_analysis/fig_action_analysis_delta.png)

Figure 6: Error analysis of decision behavior. Each group of bars shows
the change in selection rate relative to the zero-shot setting for three
action types: *optimal actions* follow the shortest path, *suboptimal
actions* are executable but deviate from the shortest path, and *invalid
actions* cannot be executed in the current state.

### 5.3 Error Analysis

#### Motivation and Setting.

The main results show that ICL and Skill Learning improve success rate,
but do not reveal what agents actually learn from experience. As defined
in
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
the action candidates at each step fall into three types: optimal
actions that follow the shortest path, suboptimal actions that are
executable but deviate from the shortest path, and invalid actions that
cannot be executed in the current state. We analyze how agents choose
among these three action types. Instead of running new experiments, we
use the selected actions recorded at each decision step in the main
experiment (all four harnesses with Qwen3.8-Flash). Specifically, we
compare the selection rate of each action type under ICL and Skill
Learning with that in the zero-shot setting.

Results and Analysis. As shown in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Motivation and Setting. ‣ 5.2 Scaling with the Number of Learning Samples ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
experience sharply reduces invalid actions across all harnesses (by
13%–20%). Fewer invalid actions allow agents to stay on executable
trajectories and reach the goal within the step budget. This suggests
that the reduction in invalid actions contributes to the higher success
rates in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Agent configurations. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents").
Meanwhile, optimal actions increase substantially. Suboptimal actions
also increase slightly (by 3%–8%). Overall, experience shifts the
selections of agents from invalid actions to optimal and suboptimal
actions. ICL and Skill Learning show the same direction of change, but
Skill Learning consistently produces smaller shifts across all
harnesses. In contrast,
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Agent configurations. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
shows no consistent advantage between ICL and Skill Learning in success
rate. This may reflect a difference in how experience is represented.
Interaction trajectories may induce larger changes in decision behavior,
while skill summaries may induce smaller but more focused changes.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.4 Step Budget Sensitivity

#### Motivation and Setting.

Each task has a shortest path to the goal, but agents often make
suboptimal decisions along the way. As described in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
agents are allowed 3 extra steps by default as a small tolerance for
suboptimal decisions. Here, we vary the number of extra steps from 0 to
6. We examine how the step budget affects success rate under different
evaluation settings. We use Hermes with Qwen3.8-Flash for this analysis.

![Refer to
caption](2610.13021v1/figure/experiment/step_budget/step_budget_sensitivity.png)

Figure 7: Step budget sensitivity. The $`x`$-axis shows the number of
extra steps allowed beyond the shortest path. By default, agents are
allowed 3 extra steps in the testing phase.

Results and Analysis. As shown in
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Motivation and Setting. ‣ 5.4 Step Budget Sensitivity ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
all three settings show a monotonically increasing success rate as the
budget grows from 0 to 6 extra steps. This is expected, since a larger
budget gives agents more room for suboptimal decisions. Across all
budget values, the ranking of the three settings remains consistent. ICL
achieves the highest success rate, followed by Skill Learning and then
zero shot. This indicates that the gain over zero shot holds across
different budgets. At the strictest budget (0 extra steps), zero-shot
success rate is 0.0%, while ICL and Skill Learning still achieve 15.0%
and 7.0%, respectively. Even under this strictest budget, learning from
experience remains effective. Notably, compared to the zero-shot
setting, ICL and Skill Learning exhibit a steeper increase in success
rate as the budget grows. This indicates that the agents with prior
experience can better benefit from additional tolerance. Meanwhile, the
gap between experienced agents and zero-shot agents remains substantial
even at the most generous budget (6 extra steps). This suggests that
additional tolerance cannot replace the role of prior experience.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 6 Conclusion

We introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first embodied simulation benchmark
for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving
agents. Our key idea is to formulate continual learning through
compositional generalization: rather than solving each new task from
scratch, an agent should accumulate experience from basic tasks and
recombine previously acquired skills to solve unseen, more complex
tasks. Following this principle, EmbodiedCLBench organizes tasks into
atomic actions, basic tasks, and advanced tasks, providing a structured
protocol for measuring whether embodied agents can acquire, retain, and
transfer experience over time.

Extensive evaluations across multiple agent harnesses and learning
methods reveal both promising progress and clear limitations: (1)
Experience from basic tasks substantially improves performance on unseen
advanced tasks over zero-shot execution, showing that current agents can
transfer previously acquired knowledge to new compositions. (2) However,
the performance of existing agents is far from saturation. Designing
effective continual learning methods for embodied agents is a promising
direction to explore. (3) Further, the benefit of learning does not
consistently increase with the amount of experience. How to enable the
agents to accumulate and exploit additional interactions is still an
open problem. Overall, EmbodiedCLBench provides a principled testbed for
studying self-evolution in embodied agents and highlights the need for
stronger mechanisms that can continuously consolidate, generalize, and
reuse experience across tasks.

## Appendix A Basic Task Categories

As described in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Task Generation: Compositional Generalization ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
basic tasks in EmbodiedCLBench span six capability categories.
Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Appendix A Basic Task Categories ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
lists each category and its core evaluation question.

|  Category |  Core Question |
|----|----|
|  Object Manipulation |  Can the agent locate and manipulate everyday objects into a usable or manageable state? |
|  Spatial Placement |  Can the agent understand spatial relationships between objects and surfaces or containers? |
|  Accessibility Control |  Can the agent change the state of doors, drawers, and cabinet doors to enable or restrict access? |
|  Appliance Operation |  Can the agent toggle household appliances and environmental devices? |
|  Activity-Driven Scene Configuration |  Can the agent set up multiple objects and devices to support activities such as reading, dining, or leisure? |
|  Household State Restoration |  Can the agent restore a room to a tidy, energy-efficient, and reusable state? |

Table 2: Six capability categories of basic tasks in EmbodiedCLBench.

## Appendix B Graph Construction Pipeline

As described in
Sections [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Task Generation: Compositional Generalization ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents")
and [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents"),
EmbodiedCLBench builds tasks from atomic actions available in TongSim.
Given the atomic actions for each task, we first construct the
state-transition graph. We then generate two types of textual content:
task descriptions and per-state action options.

#### LLM Generation.

Both task descriptions and action options are produced by a three-stage
pipeline powered by Qwen3.7-Plus. The pipeline serves two purposes:
converting low-level atomic actions into natural household scenarios,
and ensuring that action options do not give away the correct answer
through shortcuts. The key prompt specifications for all three stages
are provided in
Section [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Prompt Specifications ‣ Appendix B Graph Construction Pipeline ‣ EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents").

#### Human Verification.

Three annotators independently verify each generated sample. The
verification covers three aspects: captured images, task descriptions,
and per-state action options. For each aspect, annotators check for
factual errors, logical inconsistencies, and whether the content
reflects realistic household activities. A sample is retained only if
all three annotators approve it.

## Appendix C Task Examples

We provide task examples at both compositional levels to illustrate the
evaluation format. The agent first receives a natural-language task
description. At each step, it observes the current-state image and
selects one action from multiple candidates. Specifically, we include
two basic-task examples

|----|----|----|----|
|  State |  Option |  Text shown to the agent |  Hidden role |
|  State 0 |  A |  Head over to the ceiling light area to get ready to turn it off. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 0 |  B |  Switch on the overhead light to brighten the living room before the movie. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 0 |  C |  Shut off the ceiling light right away to set the mood for the movie. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 0 |  D |  The overhead light is still on — that’s the first thing to deal with before the movie. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 1 |  A |  Check the ceiling light to see if it’s already been switched off. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 1 |  B |  Switch off the ceiling light to darken the room for movie viewing. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 1 |  C |  Turn on the ceiling light to brighten the space before settling in for the movie. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 1 |  D |  Walk over to the ceiling light so you can reach the switch. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 2 |  A |  Switch off the overhead light — the room needs to be dark for the movie. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 2 |  B |  Step closer to the ceiling fixture to get a better grip on the switch. |  Executable detour |
|  State 2 |  C |  Glance up at the ceiling light to confirm how bright it still is. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 2 |  D |  Check the television area to see if the media setup is ready. |  Executable detour |
|  State 3 |  A |  Head over to the television area to get the media setup going. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 3 |  B |  Walk toward the ceiling light to start working on the room’s ambiance. |  Executable detour |
|  State 3 |  C |  Switch on the overhead light to brighten things up before the movie. |  Executable detour |
|  State 3 |  D |  With the light off, the media cabinet by the TV is the next thing to handle. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 4 |  A |  Power down the television to eliminate any screen glare during the movie. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 4 |  B |  Walk up to the TV unit — the cabinet is right ahead. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 4 |  C |  Focus on the television to assess whether the screen needs attention. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 4 |  D |  Switch on the television so you can test the viewing angle for the movie. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 5 |  A |  Shift your focus to the ceiling light to confirm it’s off for movie time. |  Executable detour |
|  State 5 |  B |  Open the media cabinet so everything is within reach for the movie. |  Correct shortest-path action |
|  State 5 |  C |  Take a closer look at the television area to plan the next move for the media setup. |  Invalid in current state |
|  State 5 |  D |  Step over to the television unit to get a better position for the entertainment area. |  Executable detour |
````
